newsitem.title: UK: Yorks. Water sees wide appeal for share plan.
newsitem.headline: Yorks. Water sees wide appeal for share plan.

text.p: The directors of Yorkshire Water Plc aim to give as many shareholders as possible the opportunity to take part in a cash-for-shares buyback revealed on Thursday.

Finance director Brian Wilson told reporters that, after considering special dividends and conventional buybacks, it had opted for a consolidation because "we wanted to have a method that gave all of our shareholders a chance to participate".

Under the plan, if all shareholders choose to cash in a new series of B shares at a fixed price of 36 pence each, the total cost would be 145 million stg. At the same time gearing would rise to 35 percent from the current 20 percent.
"We believe that many shareholders will choose to sell them and that is a process which will lead to more debt and less equity on the balance sheet," Wilson explained.

The plan's emphasis on smaller investors and shareholders has two key features, and the company was at pains to stress that it wanted to give a lift to its estimated 40,000 small investors in its home region of Yorkshire, northern England.

As well as giving them a fairer chance of getting back some cash than under a conventional buyback, which is mainly aimed at institutions, it was also hoped to improve the marketability of all the shares, Wilson said.

After the split and consolidation there will be 18 new shares for every 10 old ones. Any B shares not converted into cash will be eligibile for a quarterly dividend calculated not from the company's earnings performance but on a non-cumulative basis of 75 percent of the prevailing Libor rate. Asked how he expected shareholders to react to the cash and split package, which has to be approved at an extraordinary meeting on February 26, Wilson said: "We're very confident that our shareholders will find it a very attractive option."
All holders will, however, be taxed on any cash raised by their B share sale which will be treated as a disposal gain.

Yorkshire's equity base adjustment, which also adds up to an offer of a shareholder benefits package, marks a new phase for the firm. It has struggled for nearly two years to upgrade and rebuild its infrastructure after record droughts revealed big shortcomings in its ability to secure and deliver water.

During this time Yorkshire has tried to win back customer confidence and also sought to assure the country's regulator of water supplies that it is able to balance the interests of its circa two million customers with those of shareholders.
Of a capital investment programme totalling more than 300 million stg, about 230 million had been spent so far, Wilson said.
The company's reservoir stocks, at 32 percent full this time last year, are now 88 percent full, he added.
"Therefore, we feel that the security of the water supply has been taken care of, and now we can improve our financial efficiency for the benefit of shareholders," Wilson said.
He added he believed the package would be acceptable to the water regulator Ofwat.
After the announcement, Yorkshire Water's share price rose to stand up 15 pence at 732-1/2 pence by 0910 GMT.
